analysis.one_liner: Tightens FAA oversight of how aircraft makers certify their own planes, after fatal airliner crashes.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Commerce chairman with the committee's top Democrat as cosponsor, the bill cleared the Commerce Committee in November 2020 but never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After recent fatal accidents involving U.S.-built airliners exposed how much certification work the FAA delegates to the manufacturers' own employees, this bill would have tightened that system. It would have required large aircraft manufacturers to run formal safety management systems, put FAA engineers alongside the manufacturer employees who make compliance findings, banned FAA employee bonuses tied to hitting certification schedules, created an anonymous safety-reporting channel for FAA engineers, and extended whistleblower protection to employees of aircraft makers who report safety violations. It also repealed two provisions from 2018 that had encouraged faster certification.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers get an extra layer of independent scrutiny over new aircraft designs. FAA engineers and inspectors get training, anonymous reporting, and freedom from bonuses tied to certification speed. Employees of aircraft manufacturers gain legal protection if they report safety violations to their employer or the government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers and FAA safety staff

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers holding both type and production certificates to adopt a safety management system meeting international standards, backed by a continuous FAA surveillance and audit process.

Requires the FAA to assign its own aviation safety engineers as advisors to the manufacturer employees who make certification findings on the largest airliners and their engines, and to audit each certification unit at least every three years.
Prohibits the FAA from giving employees awards or bonuses for meeting schedules or quotas for certificates issued.
Creates an anonymous, non-punitive safety reporting program so FAA engineers can flag designs they believe are noncompliant or unsafe during certification.

Extends whistleblower protection to employees of aircraft, engine, and propeller manufacturers and their suppliers who report FAA safety violations, and bans performance incentives that pressure certification unit members.
Requires pilot evaluations for new passenger airliners to use pilots from the foreign and domestic airlines expected to fly them, sampled across experience levels.

analysis.who_pays: Aircraft manufacturers, chiefly makers of the largest passenger jets, bear the cost of new safety management systems, FAA audits, and advisor oversight of their certification staff. Taxpayers fund roughly $20 million a year in authorizations for FAA continuing education and technical advisors. Slower or more document-heavy certification could delay aircraft deliveries, a cost manufacturers would pass along.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the delegation program itself in place: manufacturer employees still make most day-to-day compliance findings, with FAA advisors monitoring rather than taking the work back in-house.
New safety management system rulemaking, continuous surveillance, audits, and $10 million a year each for FAA continuing education and technical advisors impose real compliance and taxpayer costs.
Many provisions are studies, reviews, and reports with deadlines stretching up to 24 months for the key safety management rule, so the safety changes would have arrived slowly even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety measures respond to a genuine, well-documented oversight problem: the bill's own text targets 'regulatory coziness' between the FAA and the manufacturers it oversees, and the 737 MAX crashes showed how dangerous that can be. The direct costs are modest relative to the industry's size, but the bill is also modest in reach — it disciplines the self-certification system rather than ending it, and much of the work would have taken years of rulemaking and reporting to land.

outcome.mechanism: The Commerce Committee approved it in November 2020, but the bill never came up for a vote in the full Senate before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, introduced the bill on June 16, 2020, with the committee's ranking Democrat, Sen. Maria Cantwell, as its only cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
On November 18, 2020, the committee ordered the bill to be reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
No further action followed; the Senate never debated or voted on the bill, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Aircraft manufacturers kept the existing certification arrangement — no mandated safety management systems, no FAA advisors attached to their certification units, no ban on certification-quota bonuses, and no new whistleblower exposure for safety reporting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Aircraft manufacturers, mainly large airliner makers

sides.party_line_note: The bill was led by the committee's Republican chairman and cosponsored by its top Democrat, and the committee reported it favorably; nothing in the record shows party-based opposition — the bill simply never got floor time in either chamber.

industries.industry: Aircraft manufacturers (especially large airliner makers like Boeing)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed new costs on manufacturers — safety management systems, continuous FAA surveillance, audits, and advisors watching their certification staff — but it keeps the delegation program under which manufacturer employees make most certification findings, locking in the industry's central role in approving its own designs. Its interest in light-touch certification runs against the independent oversight the public relies on.

The bill would require airlines to supply pilots, sampled across experience levels, for certification flight evaluations of new airliners — a modest operational burden in exchange for aircraft better tested with the crews that will fly them.
